summary: Reconsiders socket-numbering conventions. The Host-Host protocol only said the low-order bit marks socket gender. Two proposals wanted extra network-wide structure, such as a user number for accounting and access control. The authors weigh them and conclude a major NCP overhaul is needed.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC considers two proposed rules for assigning network socket numbers. It recommends waiting because the existing numbers are already limited and the changes would require broader work on NCP.

subtitle: Why two proposals for extra structure in socket numbers were set aside.

tldr.problem: Two proposals sought network-wide conventions for the 32-bit socket number, beyond the existing rule for its low-order bit.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC discusses uniqueness, repeatability and host-level allocation, and explains why a uniform division of socket fields would be difficult across different hosts.
tldr.outcome: The authors recommend setting both proposals aside until a major NCP protocol overhaul can be considered.

facts.label: Gender indicator
facts.value: Low-order bit of the socket number

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 167 as Unknown and records no RFC that updates or obsoletes it. It documents a 1971 discussion of socket-number conventions.

sections.title: The Two Proposals
sections.content:
The current NCP Protocol does not specify how hosts assign socket numbers to process ports, except that the low-order bit indicates socket gender, meaning send or receive. Two proposals called for additional network-wide rules for the 32-bit number.

One proposal reserved part of the number for a network-unique user number for accounting and access control. The other required the high-order 16 bits to be zero to reduce the socket-table space needed by smaller hosts. The RFC recommends setting both proposals aside pending consideration of a major NCP overhaul.
sections.plainLanguage: One proposal wanted socket numbers to identify users, and another wanted to limit part of the number. The authors say both should wait until the NCP is reviewed more broadly.

sections.title: Uniqueness and Repeatable Assignment
sections.content:
Socket numbers identify process ports when connections are established. They need to be unique to avoid ambiguity, and assignments should be repeatable so processes can reconnect to the same ports. Active-connection tables can check for duplicate assignments.

Some socket numbers are well-known service ports; others are supplied during an Initial Connection Protocol exchange. Concurrent copies of a program need distinct identifiers, so the system generally must allocate sockets dynamically.
sections.plainLanguage: A socket number must identify the right process without confusion. Some numbers are known in advance, while others are assigned when a connection is made.

sections.title: Managing Socket Space
sections.content:
The RFC argues against keeping a complete list of every socket assignment. With many numbers available, a host could use sparse assignments and check whether a requested number is active, reserved for a service, or permitted for the requesting process.

One suggested approach divides a host's socket space among its users and may reserve a utility partition for numbers that need not be repeatable. The RFC suggests thinking of a socket as having user, process and tag fields, but says the field divisions need not be uniform across hosts. Each host can maintain uniqueness and repeatability locally.
sections.plainLanguage: Each host could manage its socket numbers in a way that suits its own limits. The network does not need every host to divide those numbers into the same fields.

sections.title: A Possible Protocol Change
sections.content:
The RFC also records a suggestion that socket numbers may not need to remain stored for the full life of a connection, since they are used later only in the CLOSE command. A revised CLOSE using the host-line pair might let a space-limited host forget the number after connection setup.

The document raises this as a possibility rather than adopting it. It also says a more capable identification mechanism, such as hierarchical names of arbitrary length, may eventually be needed.
sections.plainLanguage: The author raises a possible way to help hosts with limited space: change CLOSE so they can forget a socket number sooner. The RFC does not specify that change.
